issues.issue: This grant defines only "Said Land," yet the operative provisions throughout (Paragraphs 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 15, 19 and 20) impose rights and duties by reference to the undefined term "Leased Premises." Whether the two terms are coextensive, and whether "Leased Premises" shrinks with the partial terminations worked by Paragraph 4, is left open.

The habendum turns on production "in commercial quantities," a phrase the lease nowhere defines despite using it as the trigger in Paragraphs 3(g), 4(a), 4(b), 4(d) and 6. Its meaning (profit over operating costs? over all costs?) is the classic point of construction in a secondary-term dispute.

The oil royalty is stated twice over and inconsistently within one sentence: "the value of the gross production" is then equated to "the proceeds received by Lessee." A market-value measure and a proceeds measure can diverge, and the sentence does not say which governs when they do.

Where Lessee itself purchases the royalty oil there is no third-party sale, so the price term "at the same proceeds received by Lessee for the sale thereof" is circular. It is unclear whether Lessee must pay a market or arm's-length price or may set the price by its own purchase.

The transportation carve-out is grammatically broken ("Any deduction for the expenses ... shall be added to the price received" with an unclosed parenthetical reading "limited to direct for amounts of Lessor's gas transported"), so the scope of the permitted regulated-pipeline deduction cannot be read off the words. Whether "gathering" and "compression" charged by an affiliate midstream company fall inside or outside the no-deduction rule is the central ambiguity.

The royalty base is "proceeds received from any sale of such gas at the point of sale or delivery," which sits against Paragraph 3(f)'s command that royalties be delivered free of gathering, compression, treating and marketing costs "except as provided for in 3(b)." The two must be reconciled to know whether the valuation point can be moved downstream by netting costs out of the sale price.

The floor is set by "proceeds received from sales in the field or prevailing area whichever is the greater," and neither "field" nor "prevailing area" is defined or bounded. Nor is it said whose sales, over what period, are to be compared.

The trigger — gas "sufficiently impregnated" that "paying quantities" can be liquefied "as a practical lease operation" — states no measurable threshold and leaves the duty to install separators to argument. Whether Lessee ever owed the installation obligation is therefore indeterminate on the face of the clause.

The clause forbids "any deductions for any indirect or direct costs" but then supplies a parenthetical list ("amortization and depreciation on pipeline and plant investment and indirect overhead associated therewith"), inviting the argument that only the enumerated costs are barred. The general ban and the specific enumeration cannot both be given full effect.

The floor requires computing "the royalties that would have been paid ... under Paragraph 3(b) if the gas were marketed pursuant to such Paragraph 3(b)," a counterfactual the clause gives no method for calculating. Whether the comparison uses actual residue-gas prices, field prices, or the 3(b) minimum-proceeds test is unstated.

"Free use ... for operations hereunder" does not say whether it reaches only operations on Said Land or extends to operations on pooled lands or off-lease facilities such as compressors and plants. The boundary of the free-use privilege is the ambiguity.

Computing royalty after deducting production used is in tension with Paragraph 3(f), which requires royalties to be delivered free of production, compression, treating and processing costs. Whether fuel gas burned in compression is a permitted volumetric deduction or a forbidden cost is the question.

The blanket no-cost rule is subject to an exception "except as provided for in 3 (b) above," but Paragraph 3(b) is itself a no-deduction provision containing only a narrow regulated-transportation carve-out. What that cross-reference excepts — the regulated transportation charges only, or all costs netted from 3(b) proceeds — is the point a court would have to construe.

Shut-in royalty is available for wells "capable of producing gas in commercial quantities," an undefined standard that does not say whether capability is measured with or without pipeline connection and marketing facilities. The lease's continuance under Paragraph 4(d) turns on that same untested phrase.

The renewal deadline — "yearly on or before the expiration of the last day of the year following the preceding year for which such payment or tender has been made" — is circular and does not identify the anniversary date. It cannot be squared word-for-word with the preceding sentence's "at yearly intervals" after a ninety-day first payment.

This sentence caps post-primary-term shut-in maintenance at "two consecutive years," but the next sentences (3(g) increased $750 payment and the three-year cumulative cap) presuppose shut-in maintenance continuing past two years. The two-year limit and the three-year limit cannot both be given effect.

"Drilling unit" is fixed to Section 15-72-302 of the Arkansas Code, yet Paragraph 4(g) permits a retained drilling unit to include additional acreage when a larger spacing pattern is prescribed. Which meaning controls when a field-wide order enlarges units is unresolved.

The escalation to $750 "[f]ollowing the expiration of the two (2) year shut-in period" assumes the lease survives that period, while the immediately preceding sentence says shut-in payment maintains the lease "for a period not to exceed two consecutive years." The increased-payment sentence has no field of operation unless that cap is read away.

This three-year cumulative cap contradicts the earlier sentence of 3(g) limiting post-primary-term shut-in maintenance to two consecutive years. A court would have to decide whether the outer limit is two years or three.

Exempting shut-in payments from proportionate reduction cannot easily be squared with Paragraph 5's rule that on pooled production Lessor receives only its acreage share, or with Paragraph 16's proportionate-reduction covenant. Whether a full $500 per well is owed where Lessor owns a fractional or pooled interest is open.

"[T]hirty (30) days following ... receipt ... of proceeds ... but no later than one hundred eighty (180) days after the date of first production, whichever is the earliest" pits a floor against a ceiling and then calls for the "earliest" of them. The sentence does not say which date governs when receipt of proceeds comes after the 180th day.

"[I]nterest at ten percent (10%) per annum for each day overdue to a maximum of one hundred, twenty (120) days" is ambiguous as to whether the 120-day cap limits the days interest accrues or something else, and "per annum for each day" is internally inconsistent. The rate may also collide with Arkansas's usury ceiling.

Declaring the royalty obligation "absolute and unconditional" and immune from "any defense (other than payment)" is difficult to reconcile with Paragraph 16, which reduces royalties proportionately to Lessor's fractional interest and disclaims title warranty. Whether Lessee may adjust payments for title failure despite this clause is the question.

Saying the take-in-kind option may be exercised "at any time, and from time to time" on sixty days' notice conflicts with the last sentence of 3(i), which makes any election effective "for a period of not less than twelve (12) months." The frequency with which Lessor may switch is left contradictory.

"[A]t Lessor's option, at the wellhead after separation and dehydration" gives an option but names only one delivery point, leaving unclear what the alternative is. It also does not say who bears separation and dehydration costs for in-kind gas.

Charging Lessor with "[a]ll other costs and expenses attributable to" separate marketing sits against Paragraph 3(f), which requires royalty production to reach Lessor free of gathering, compression, treating and transportation costs. Which costs shift on an in-kind election is unresolved between the two.

A twelve-month minimum election period cannot be squared with the earlier sentence of 3(i) permitting exercise "at any time, and from time to time" on sixty days' notice. The lease does not say which limit prevails on a rapid switch back and forth.

Paragraph 2 continues the lease so long as "drilling or reworking operations are conducted thereon," while 4(a) continues it only if Lessee "is then engaged in drilling operations" at the very moment the Primary Term expires. Whether operations commenced after expiration can save the lease depends on which provision controls.

The lease is continued "in the manner and for the time specified in Paragraph 4" — a reference back to the whole of the paragraph of which this sentence is part, naming no subparagraph. The circular cross-reference leaves the applicable holding period unidentified.

This clause requires drilling operations to proceed "with no cessation of more than thirty (30) consecutive days," while Paragraph 4(c) defines reasonable diligence for all purposes of the lease as no cessation of more than sixty (60) consecutive days. A forty-day gap satisfies one provision and breaches the other.

This sixty-day definition of "reasonable diligence" is stated to govern "[f]or all purposes of this Lease," yet Paragraph 4(b) requires the same diligence with no cessation exceeding thirty days. The two definitions of the permitted gap cannot both stand.

Commencement is defined solely by the drilling bit penetrating the surface, but Paragraph 4(c) defines "drilling operations" to include reworking, deepening, plugging back and cleaning out, which involve no new surface penetration. The definition and the operations it purports to date do not fit, and 4(c)(iv) supplies a different rule for "all other operations."

"Upon expiration of the Primary Term and completion of continuous drilling operations" states two triggers without saying whether both must occur, so the date on which the lease contracts to producing units is indeterminate. Paragraph 4(e) meanwhile keeps the whole lease alive during continuous drilling, making the moment of partial termination a matter of construction.

The trigger is "completion of operations under Paragraph 4(c)(ii) or 4(c)(iii)," but those subparagraphs merely fix completion dates and describe no operations. The mis-citation leaves the starting point of the continuous-drilling period uncertain.

A 120-day gap is permitted between wells here, while Paragraph 4(b) tolerates no cessation of more than thirty days and Paragraph 4(c) no more than sixty. Which interval measures Lessee's continuity after the Primary Term is unclear.

The depth-severance sentence is self-contradictory: it first terminates the lease below 100 feet under the deepest production casing, then provides that where "no productive perforated interval exists" the same termination occurs "thereupon" as to later-completed wells. The date and the depth of the deep-rights termination cannot be fixed from the words.

Allowing a retained drilling unit to include "as much additional surface acreage as may be so prescribed or permitted" conflicts with Paragraph 3(g), which fixes "drilling unit" to the meaning in Ark. Code § 15-72-302. Whether enlarged units hold additional acreage under Paragraph 4(d) turns on that clash.

The duty to form units so as to "best utilize all available acreage" is qualified by "to the extent a reasonable prudent Operator would do so," a standard that may swallow the obligation entirely. Neither "best utilize" nor the prudent-operator qualifier gives a measurable benchmark.

This clause permits cessations of restoration operations of up to sixty days, while Paragraph 4(b) allows no cessation of more than thirty consecutive days in restoring production. Which grace period saves a unit after production ceases is contested between them.

Pooling is committed to "Lessee's judgment" that it is "necessary or advisable," with the land limited to tracts "adjoining or in the immediate vicinity thereof" — neither the discretion nor the geographic limit is bounded. Whether pooling must also be exercised in good faith and what counts as "immediate vicinity" are open.

Gas units "shall not exceed the number of acres specified for a gas well drilling unit," but the clause never says specified where — by the Arkansas Commission, by § 15-72-302, or by Paragraph 4(g). The acreage cap therefore has no ascertainable figure.

Treating pooled operations as if they occurred on Said Land "for all purposes hereof" conflicts with the later sentence of Paragraph 5 providing that, notwithstanding anything to the contrary, pooled operations maintain the lease only as to acreage inside the unit. The scope of the deemed-production rule depends on which sentence yields.
